utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Good afternoon to everyone. May we have the appearances today, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everyone. I'm Tom Hannis, along with Crispian Smith for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, Eugene O'Sullivan, Ms. Tatjana Savic, and we are joined with our interns, Amanda Gruenhagen and Fernando Dutra, all appearing for Stanisic Defence this afternoon. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic and Aleksandar Aleksic, appearing for Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, I would like to report that I am also present here. I'm always left out of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cvijetic. Before the usher escorts the witness back to the stand, Mr. Hannis, the -- when we were calculating the time that this witness -- that would be needed to complete this witness's testimony, as is the usual practice, the calling party having indicated 20 hours, the like amount of time was anticipated by the Prosecution. The -- in fact, Mr. Zecevic spent 12 hours, and is there any reason why the Chamber should be thinking in terms of your spending a greater amount of time than that in your current examination of cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, in that 12 hours, the witness covered a lot of territory. I think during the Prosecution's case in-chief there were a number of times where cross-examination exceeded the time in direct. I -- I personally find I'm having some difficulty in getting short answers to questions, so it is taking me longer than I anticipated. Also, a number of the answers, as you've seen, I have been adding documents almost daily and that's in part because of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]... one of the reasons that prompted our question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. It is because I get an answer to a question which opens the door that I feel I need to address. It -- when I'm expecting the answer to be perhaps, I don't know, I get an answer that, I do know because of X, Y, and Z. And then I find myself in the position that I feel I need to go and find a document that addresses X, Y, and Z. This is the last Defence witness. In some ways, in my personal view, he is more of an expert on police matters than the designated police expert was, and I think the time -- the extra time that I'm asking to have with this witness will be well-spent and useful to Your Honours in making your final assessment in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So where -- where do you project -- how much longer do you project your cross-examination to be, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I was informed that I think I've spent 8 hours and 9 minutes up to this point in time. And judging by the page number I'm on and the page number I have to go to in my notes, I'm a little less than halfway, so I projected that I would need another 10 or 12 hours, which would take us into Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. This is a matter to which we may have to return, but thank you, Mr. Hannis. Could the usher please escort the witness back to the stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, Mr. Macar. I remind you you're still on your oath.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Macar, yesterday near the end of the day, I asked you about RS Assembly sessions you attended in 1992. I think we established that you may have attended only one, that being in December. But other than yourself, do you know what MUP, RS MUP personnel, attended Assembly sessions in 1992? And I mean apart from Minister Stanisic, who is reflected in -- in one or two of the Assembly sessions as having been present and spoken. But anyone else in the RS MUP who attended Assembly sessions in 1992?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall whether there were any other representative presents -- well, that depended on the topic discussed. When crime was discussed, I was there. And the operational and counter-sabotage section, parts of the administration and the relevant centres and public security stations were represented. Now, as for which other senior officers from the MUP headquarters were present there, I don't really know. I can't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. The last document I think we looked at yesterday was the one signed by Mr. Trbojevic over the typewritten name of Mr. Djeric, addressed to Mr. Kljajic about investigations related to the vehicles from TAS, the car factory in Vogosca. My question for you today is: Did you never hear it mentioned in 1992 that Momcilo Mandic and/or Dusko Malovic and some of his men from the special police platoon were involved in taking cars from TAS?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the operational materials, I don't think that any mention was made of Mr. Mandic and Mr. Malovic. And now whether there was any speculation in the public or in some circles, it's possible, but I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in the operational material, as far as what was happening to the cars that were being taken from there, did you have information that many of them were being taken to Serbia and sold?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, some of the cars were sold in Serbia. I already said that in my evidence. And this prompted us to contact the Serbian MUP, seeking assistance from them. We wanted to give them the data about the number of vehicles that we had gathered until that time, and all the other details so that they could take appropriate measures to identify any such vehicles that may have been registered in the meantime in the territory of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And did you receive information that -- that some of the cars from TAS that had been sold in Serbia, the proceeds from such sales were being used to buy equipment for the RS MUP?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that some stations received approval from the Crisis Staffs to sell a certain number of vehicles in order to obtain, to procure equipment. Some of it went to the MUP; some perhaps to the municipality; and maybe even to the army. But there were such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But did know about cases where -- where MUP headquarters and/or the special police, under Mr. Karisik had permission to take cars from TAS and sell them in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that Mr. Karisik, who was commander of the special police brigade, had permission to sell cars in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Or anyone else in the MUP headquarters?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. And it was not usual practice for anyone from the MUP headquarters to sell cars.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Last week, at page 22927, regarding the problem with the stolen cars, you said that one of the ideas proposed by the minister of the interior was to "relocate the vehicles to a safe territory" and put under the jurisdiction of the commodity reserves administration of Republika Srpska. Can you tell us some details about when and where and how this idea was proposed by the minister?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the first information came in that in the Vogosca municipality in the TAS factory compound there was a large number of already-assembled vehicles, Golf cars, and that people started taking those vehicles away on various grounds. And that the factory was in a combat zone. The minister's associates made this proposal, and the conclusion reached by the minister and his associates was that, in a combat zone, it would be difficult to provide appropriate, physical security for those vehicles in the whole compound where the vehicles were located. And as far as I can recall, a small military unit secured the TAS factory in April and May, but they did not have enough personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the minister proposed --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I wanted to stop you there because you're telling me the why, but my question was: When and where and how was this proposal made? Could you please answer those questions for me.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I really tried, and I do apologise for being too extensive. I tried to give you an explanation --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand that --

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- why --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- but I was just asking, when, where, and how. Can you answer those first?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: How: Based on the reported that we received, the minister and his associates concluded that a proposal be made to the government, to relocate the vehicles to a safer area and to place them under the control of the relevant state authorities who were able to perform this task and do it in accordance with the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. You've answered how and to whom. Can you tell me when this proposal was made and where it was made? Was it made orally; was it made in writing?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was May, and the minister -- well, I don't remember any written documents, although there had been an extensive correspondence about the TAS case, but the minister was able to present to the government at the session of the government, or to the prime minister, this proposal. So he could do it orally or in writing. Because that's the way the communication goes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. So, as far as you know, there's no written proposal reflecting this; right? You've not seen such a document.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was no need for any kind of written document because it could have been done orally. An oral proposal could be made at the session of the government or proposed to the prime minister and there was no need to have paperwork. You could just say that there is a great value in those cars, and this had to be relocated in order to safe-guard it. This was the general position of the ministry, not only when it came to the TAS factory, but for all the depots or warehouses where valuable goods were stored, and it was impossible, because of the war and lack of personnel, to secure them properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could have a look at Exhibit 1D93. This was Defence tab 44.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Macar, you will see this is a document dated 29 July 1992 from you to the chiefs of several SJBs, the administration for financial affairs, the special purposes police detachment CSB at Sarajevo, and the minister himself for information. Do you remember sending this document out in connection with the TAS investigation?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if you could look at the bottom -- or the last paragraph above your signature. It's page 2 of the English, and in e-court, page 2 of the B/C/S as well. My last paragraph translation reads: "Report on vehicles sold by the SJB and special police detachment in order to acquire materiel and technical equipment and the like." That suggests to me that you were already aware in late July 1992 that the special police had sold certain Golf vehicles -- or certain vehicles from TAS. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Then --

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I can give you an explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, yes, that's my question then. If you didn't have that information, why are you asking the question about reporting on vehicles sold by them?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: This part of the document was phrased in this way because there were some reports regarding -- from some of the SJBs. And since there were some speculations that the ministry was involved in all this, to the effect that the ministry itself had stolen the vehicles and disposed of them, and the purpose of those speculations, of course, was entirely different. We demanded that all public security stations and the police detachment whose elements were deployed in the Sarajevo area to check whether they had sold any such vehicles, and if yes, to provide this kind of information. So this went for all the SJBs, although we did have some information already for some of the public security stations, such as Vogosca.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And in an answer you gave last week, you said: "This operation continued for a number of years." When was it finally completed, if ever?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, since this was active, I'm sure that in 1997 [as interpreted], there were some cases where vehicles were found in Montenegro or Serbia, Bosnia-Herzegovina. The information was coming in, and in those isolated cases -- well, the search for those vehicles was ongoing. It was still active. And if any information came in, indicating that there was such a case, checks were always run. This was not something that demanded the entire ministry and the centres to be involved because people who are operatives, they only do this kind of work and nothing else. So if a -- two such vehicles are identified somewhere, checks were run to see how the vehicles were obtained, and it is enough for a single inspector to do it. They can do it in a very short time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In the course of the investigation, how many RS MUP personnel were ever implicated and/or charged in connection with the taking of vehicles from TAS?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: After 19 years, I really can't tell you how many. But there were quite a few.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall any of them being from the special police? Either Mr. Karisik's special police or Mr. Malovic's special police platoon.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: As regards the special unit, well, I don't really recall. I don't know what you mean when you say, "Mr. Malovic's special police platoon." I don't recall that anyone from that group had ever been accused of this. I really don't recall because there were so many people working in the ministry. I can't really say. But it was determined that they were selling those cars. Some of them were identified, and criminal reports were filed against them. But now I can't really tell you whether somebody from the Sekovici SJB or this organisational unit or that. Nineteen years have passed, after all. I would have to look at some documents and then -- to jog my memory. I think that very few people would be able to recall those details after 19 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, you are the guy who could remember receiving 31 dispatches in 1992. So I thought you might remember if there was anybody from the special police who was implicated in this. You mentioned nobody from Malovic but you didn't specifically answer my question about Mr. Karisik's special police. Anyone from that unit implicated, or charged, or disciplined?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I've already responded to that question. Given the time-lapse, I really can't say who it was and from which organisational unit, because there were so many employees. I can really say whether it was from Vlasenica, Sekovici. After 19 years, it is absurd to even think that I could remember. And as regards the dispatches, the number of dispatches, Your Honours, many bad things which were a professional disgrace. I had records from April 1992 to 1999 containing 30 or 31 dispatches, and this is something that really left a bad taste in my mouth, and it's still going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I want to ask you specifically about someone else. Malko Koroman. Did you ever have any information that he or any of his employees were involved in taking vehicles from TAS factory?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: When it comes to aggravated theft, stealing cars from the TAS compound, and as for Malko and somebody else from that police station going to steal vehicles, I had no information to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you not have some information that some Golf vehicles were seized from Mr. Koroman and a couple of his colleagues by the Yellow Wasps at that check-point in Zvornik? You didn't see that information that came out during the interviews of the arrested Yellow Wasps in early August 1992?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: When it comes to the Pale station and the Yellow Wasps, yes, I'm -- I know that the Pale station gave a certain amount of weapons to the members of the Yellow Wasps group. Based on the information collected by us from SJBs, and this fell in the jurisdiction of the Bijeljina police station to whom we provided assistance, we who worked in the administration, there were five or six Golf vehicles that they seized at the check-point, manned by Yellow Wasps, as military police. There were additional two vehicles who had been seized, but I think that members of that unit actually took them to Serbia. I remember that because that was the first Golf model that was a four-wheel drive. On that occasion, we identified five or six vehicles that had been seized by the Yellow Wasps. When working with that unit, I don't think we ever came across any documents indicating from whom the Golf vehicles had been seized. The Golf vehicles that we found with them were without licence plates, and we were able to establish their origin based on the numbers in the engine. And we thus established that those vehicles came from the TAS factory and that they had been seized from the TAS compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You don't recall seeing in the statements any of the Yellow Wasps that they had, indeed, originally seized some cars from Mr. Koroman and his colleagues but then, after discussions, returned, at least a couple of them, which is why Mr. Koroman was willing to provide those men with weapons when they came to Pale later. You don't remember seeing that in the statements, the interviews taken?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for them seizing vehicles from Mr. Koroman, I can't remember that after all this time. A number of statements had been taken, over 80. But what I remember are the weapons provided by the Pale station and given to some members of that unit. There were 80, perhaps even 100 statements taken, together with amendments.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand there were several statements taken. But you, as the policeman in the crime administration, certainly would have been interested in the information that a chief of a SJB was giving weapons to non-policemen. Wouldn't that -- wouldn't the mere distribution of weapons to someone who is not in the police by Mr. Koroman have been a violation of the Law on Internal Affairs or some police regulation?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for your previous question, let me tell you, I never took any statements personally. It's just that inspectors told me about it in meetings. And as soon we learned that Mr. Koroman had given some weapons to somebody in the Yellow Wasps, we conveyed that information. We did not conceal it. We naturally informed the head of the public security department, who, at the time, was in Bijeljina, and even in the reports we submitted, both in the beginning, upon learning about this, and at the end, we included this. And it was the head of the public security department who, in his line of work -- who was in charge of organising further investigation concerning those weapons, and I believe that he, in fact, did it, via the Sarajevo centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, Mr. Koroman never got disciplined, or removed from the MUP, or criminally prosecuted for that activity, did he?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I remember is that the minister tried to remove Mr. Koroman from office in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. And that was in April 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Months before this event. Did he try to remove him after August 1992?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Because once I learned about this event, I contacted Mr. Cedo Kljajic, who was head of the public security department, and he was my immediate superior and was in Bijeljina at the time. If I may add just one sentence. Disciplinary proceedings cannot be instituted based on only one piece of information. Additional checks need to be carried out in order to institute either disciplinary proceedings or criminal proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. We saw earlier when you testified your role in a commission to investigate certain activities by Mr. Kljajic and Dragan Andan in Bijeljina, in connection with matters that eventually led to disciplinary action at least against Mr. Andan. Was there any commission formed to investigate Mr. Koroman that you know of?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you know, I spent August in Bijeljina. Perhaps even early September. And then there was a move to Pale and back to Bijeljina. I apologise. If I could have some water, please. Therefore, I cannot say with certainty whether the CSB or the head of the public security department did anything, whether he ordered the CSB to carry out some measures because the CSB had jurisdiction over the SJB and whether he asked for proceedings, be it disciplinary or criminal, to be instituted against [Realtime transcript read in error "by"] Mr. Koroman. Let me just correct something that you have mentioned. When it comes to Mr. Dragan Andan and Mr. Cedo Kljajic, perhaps I didn't explain that enough. But concerning the disciplinary proceedings against Mr. Andan, pursuant on the information that came from some figures in Bijeljina, we learned that Mr. Andan used a piece of equipment - I think it was a poker machine - in a house. And since it already leaked through the media, and there was a member of the ministry who had come to Bijeljina to improve the law and order that had been disrupted, so the minister instructed that checks be made concerning this poker machine. Based on what we learned, it seems that the rules of procedure were not complied with, based on the rules in the ministry that regulate the operations. I absolutely do not doubt the honest intentions of Mr. Andan, but when means of that nature are used, there has to be a certain criminal procedure followed, explaining why things are done in a certain way. This is according to the rules that exist within the ministry. The mere fact that somebody --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, first of all, how much longer are you going to pursue this matter of the TAS cars? And, secondly, I think you should keep your witness focussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I wasn't talking about the TAS cars anymore. Now I was talking about the failure to discipline Mr. Koroman. But I take your point. I will try and get him to limit his answers as best he can.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Sorry, Mr. Hannis. I just have one intervention in the transcript. 14:22, he says here, "... be it disciplinary or criminal, to be instituted by Mr. Koroman." I think "against Mr. Koroman" would be -- was the answer. I know that is what the witness said. He said "against Mr. Koroman," not "by Mr. Koroman."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That makes sense to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But, Mr. Macar, as a professional policeman with many years of experience, would you agree with me that there seems to be some disproportionate treatment here? Mr. Andan was disciplined for some technical misuse of a poker machine, for which the evidence shows he had authorisation from Mr. Kljajic to use in some sort of undercover investigation; whereas, Mr. Koroman, who, at the minimum, was giving weapons, and I think the weapons are listed in a document we have, including automatic weapons; I think at least one hand-held rocket-launcher. And nothing happened to him. Would you agree that seems disproportionate?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you only about the events that I took part in, and those are the checks made concerning Mr. Andan. Since the head of the administration is not authorised to institute disciplinary proceedings and, in addition to that, I was also a co-ordinator, then what the head of the public security department did in relation to the SCB that has -- SCB -- CSB that has jurisdiction over SJB, I really don't know, because the crime administration is not authorised to institute disciplinary proceedings against chiefs of SJBs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm not sure you -- you understood me question. It just -- I'm asking your opinion as a professional policeman whether it's a more serious matter for a SJB chief to give weapons to unauthorised personnel, particularly unauthorised personnel like the Yellow Wasps, who were known to have been engaged in illegal activity, as opposed to a policeman who fails to properly use a poker machine that he has been authorised to use for an undercover investigation. Can you answer that question? Doesn't the first one seem to be a more serious violation?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: If Mr. Koroman did provide weapons at the time when the public security department had information incriminating members of Yellow Wasps, then that is certainly a more serious violation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I want to move to Exhibit 1D58. This was Defence tab 36. Did you find that one?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is an order from the minister which says: "Proceeding from conclusions reached at the meeting of executive employees ... on 11 July ... the meeting of the collegiate body on 23 July and the minister's act 01-57 ... as well as other conclusions," he orders legal measures to be taken against all MUP members who have committed crimes and that they should be dismissed. I'm curious. There's a reference to a collegium meeting on the 23rd of July which is not a meeting for which we have a document. But do you recall attending that meeting? I believe, based on other evidence we've heard in the case, this is probably the last one that Mr. Planojevic attended as head of the crime administration. It was about 12 days after the Belgrade meeting. Do you remember a collegium that you would have attended on the 23rd of July?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: You said -- you asked something about Mr. Planojevic and then you asked me about whether I remembered the collegium that I attended. I can't really tell you whether I attended it or not. I need to see the agenda. Until I see the minutes from the session, it's hard for me to say what transpired there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I don't know either because I don't have the document. But, do you recall, were you in attendance at the meeting when Mr. Planojevic last was in his position as the head of the crime administration? I don't know if you were at the meeting because, I think, Mr. Stanisic already knew at that time that Planojevic was leaving, and so I wondered if you, perhaps, were invited to the meeting because it was envisioned that you would be taking over?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is quite possible that I attended the meeting, but I would like to see the minutes, just to see what topics were covered, because that would trigger my memory. All minutes indicate who attended the meeting. As for the order, I am familiar with these matters because at least a dozen times these matters were discussed, be it in short meetings with the minister, or just in passing, or within administrations, and with colleagues. These were constant topics that we discussed, and there were a number of documents sent out on these matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Perhaps, Your Honours, this is an appropriate time for our first break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Very well. We reconvene in 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: While the witness is coming in, Your Honours, I wondered if you might give me some guidance about how much time you will allow me, because if I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We intend to respond to that, but we'll do it when the witness is present so the witness would have an understanding as to how much longer he will be with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Before you continue, Mr. Hannis, and we are saying this so that the witness can be aware of this as well, the -- returning to the matter that was raised at the beginning of today's sitting, in terms of the length of time that you anticipate your cross-examination would take, we have considered what you indicated to us, and we have determined that we expect that you should complete your cross-examination in the course of Monday so that Mr. Zecevic can be begin his re-examination of the witness on Monday, and the witness would, by everything being considered, be away and released on Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Macar, yesterday, we touched briefly upon the time-period in the early August 1992, when I suggested to you that there was quite a bit of media activity relating to the existence and the conditions in -- in camps, or collection centres, or detention facilities, whatever name you may prefer, in Manjaca and Omarska. And I want to show you a document that I think followed closely on that event.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It's Exhibit P192. This is at Prosecution tab 86.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have the hard copy, if the usher would assist me in handing it to you. It's only two pages, but it may be easier to work with. It's dated the 8th of August, 1992, and I will tell you that that's -- that's one day after public announcement by Mr. Djeric, the prime minister, reacting to a CNN report about Omarska and Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, for the record, that is Exhibit P179.23.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: On the back page, you will see this comes from Tomo Kovac. You know who he is and was at the time. I believe this was at the very first day or two that he was in his new position as the assistant minister for police duties and tasks. Do you recall when he started in that job? Did you see him that day? Or were you still working on the Yellow Wasps case on the 8th of August?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that Mr. Kovac worked on the Yellow Wasps case. Now we're talking about Bijeljina, right, at the time when I was there. Now, as to when he was appointed assistant minister, whether it was in the middle of that year, I can't really tell you the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think we have another document on that in -- in evidence. But we can see that apparently by the 8th of August, he is in that position because that's the title we see by his name on the back page; right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. You see in the first paragraph he is talking about a way, perhaps, to solve problems related to the keeping of members of other ethnicities in the facilities and collection centres located in war zones. And he is proposing that the status of these people be legally altered. Do you -- do you know what he meant about that? What was their status before the 8th of August?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't speculate as to what he thought. I can assume that perhaps something was not really proper, whether it was improper in terms of procedure or documents, I can't really speculate, because I did not see any of the materials and I did not take part in the drafting of the materials, so I did not take part in it at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay let me read part of the next paragraph and ask you a question related to that. It says: "The basic problem in the field is that not all the responsible bodies are advised in the procedure of receiving such persons and their further treatment, so there are cases when members of the Ministry of the Interior receive, and sometimes even participate in the actual capture of persons in areas of combat activities, and then continue to organise their accommodation and living conditions, the period of detention and their entire fate." Now, to me, it seems like he is suggesting that part of the problem is that some of these people who are taken in, in areas where combat activities are going, are being detained under circumstances where perhaps they ought not to be detained because there's no evidence they've participated in a crime. They appear to be civilians. And they're being detained for more than three days without any criminal charges being filed. All those would be contrary to the established procedures of the Ministry of Internal Affairs; right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would need this more closely. So if I may be allowed to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sure, take your time.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can see, it says here "cases in which personnel of the Ministry of the Interior accept, or receive ...," and it doesn't say here from whom they receive, "and sometimes even take part in the actual capture of persons in areas of combat activities ..." I can't now speculate whether there were some combat operations in the immediate vicinity of which, or in the location where they went on, whether there were any other persons, or whether captured soldiers were there, I can't really read this from here. And then it goes on to say and they organised their accommodation and living conditions ... I did not know that police in Republika Srpska had sites, facilities to which they brought prisoners or civilians who were in the combat zones and whether they were held there as perpetrators of crimes, because that might be an explanation. If they committed crimes, then we can talk about some kind of a legal basis, the -- which is the provision that they may be kept in custody for up to three days.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If you'll go on to the next paragraph you see Mr. Kovac says that he believed part of the problem is there are insufficient categorisation of people in these facilities and reception centres. And he talks about three categories: Prisoners of war, who are entitled to certain kinds of treatment under the Geneva Conventions; persons who committed crimes; and, third, the civilian population. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it. And I would like to see the information based on which Mr. Kovac received the data. What kind of persons were actually detained in those collection centres.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'd like to ask him that, too. The -- the next paragraph -- the second paragraph following -- if you go to the second page for you, I think it starts at the top of the back page. It says: "The civilian population, despite belonging to another ethnic group whose extremists are at war with the Serbian Republic of BH can only be considered refugees under somewhat stricter control of the Serbian Ministry of the Interior." And it talks about accommodation of some of these persons being carried out by charitable organisations and certain local authorities. But if you could go to the next-to-the-last paragraph, then he says, "I am presenting this problem in this way because" -- and this is page 2 of the English: "Because the international institutions will not accept any other treatment of members of other ethnic groups, regardless of the situation our people face under the rule of Muslim and Croatian authorities." So, sounds like, he is concerned about the fact that Serbs being held prisoners by the Muslims and Croats are not being treated the way civilians should be treated. But, nevertheless, he feels that in the RS, civilians, even though they may be members of an ethnic group who is at war with the Republika Srpska, need to be treated in a way that the international institutions will accept. Do you disagree with that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, just as my assessments sometimes are too broad, this one is too. I would like to go back to what is written here. The problem is presented in this manner, it says here, because the international institutions will not accept any other kind of treatment of people from other ethnic communities, so we're not talking about prisoners or civilians who were in collection centres. And further up in the text that you quoted, Mr. Kovac states that the control of the Serbian ministry should be stepped up. I think that this is a reference to the need to ensure the safety of the sites where civilians were. So I would like to see what this report is based on, what this document is based on, although I can't see anything in this text which would indicate that the police, at least in most of this text except for the first part, the way that the police treated those people. And even in that part of the text, the operation of the public security station that were under increased influence of the Crisis Staffs which, in fact, perhaps I could go as far as saying that they controlled them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I believe that --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You -- I have to stop you because I have limited time and you've gone beyond my question which simply was: Do you disagree with that? And I take it you do disagree. Let me ask you though, do you recall looking at the minutes from the 11th of July meeting in Belgrade of the MUP senior staff. And I showed you the portion where Mr. Zupljanin was talking about the problem of the army and the Crisis Staffs wanting to bring in as many Muslims as possible and putting them in these undefined camps, many times in bad living conditions. Don't you think that's part of what Mr. Kovac is talking about here, the situation where the army and the Crisis Staffs are rounding up as many non-Serbs as possible and sticking them in camps and sometimes leaving the police with the dirty work of guarding those people, being held in the camps till they were either exchanged or allowed to move out, in some fashion?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't say this is a leading question. Perhaps the report, and perhaps some other reports were used by Mr. Kovac. Now whether the minutes -- I can't really speculate on his behalf.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Let me show you something different. This is 1D59. It's Defence tab 37. I think that's in your binder. This is a document dated the 23rd -- or, I'm sorry, the 24th of July, 1992. It's over the typed name of Mico Stanisic. But I think you told us this is actually your signature for Minister Stanisic; right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And can you tell us how you were given authority to sign for him? Was that in writing, or was that orally?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Orally, on the spot, in the building where we were. And let me address the Honourable Trial Chamber because we always have to go back to the 29, 31. You can see on the 24th of July the log number is 11. So in July, you have number 11, from the crime enforcement service or section log-book. Because now we can go back to this old story about 29 or 31 dispatches.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And how often did you -- or were you authorised to sign for the minister in 1992? Was this the only time that you did it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But one, two, or three, I can't really recall. I do remember this particular case. So if you're asking me about a number, not many. And in practice, the minister would issue such documents. We did not have technical capabilities. The minister did not have his associates and his whole office to order them what to type and then to sign it. He would use those administration heads who were present, and that's why you have among the signatories the gentleman from the analysis section and so on, whoever was present at the time. Whoever was in a meeting with the minister at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Going back to the number of 31, when you gave that answer as -- I'll check the transcript if you disagree, but I understood what you had said about the number 31 was 31 was the number of dispatches that you received in the crime administration in 1992. But now, you are talking about it as though 31 is the number that you sent out from your administration. Which is it? Is it those that you sent out or those that were received?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both documents that were sent and received. Not only the dispatches but also reports in writing so the total number is between 29 and 31. That covers all the documents. Documents that came in, because, at that time, whoever was this charge entered everything in the same log-book, in the same protocol. The things that came in, and those that were sent out.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Well, then you're saying, in 1992, a total number of dispatches, both incoming and outgoing, added up together, those that relate to your crime administration, totals 31, or 29 to 31; is that right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: From April to October. Not just dispatches. I'm referring to all the written documents that came in and out -- and went out. And there are records in the crime police administration concerning this. There are records to this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, before -- I think a couple of times when you talked about this, you were saying for 1992. Now you're [indiscernible] it to October.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, no, I'm sorry. Mr. Hannis, I can give you the reference where the witness said -- and it was actually your question yesterday when the witness explained that how he knows that is from the notebook that they needed to renew once they came into the -- into Bijeljina on the 3rd of October. So, therefore, it is not -- what you just said is not what the witness actually claimed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm talking about the first time he answered the question about how many documents, on direct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But let's get it straight right now. You're talking about the period between April and October 1992, and you say the total number of dispatches sent and received by your administration was between 29 and 31. Is that what you are telling us?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dispatches and memos, various documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: One of the documents we looked at earlier today was the document from you to several SJBs, to the special police detachment, to the minister for his information only, requesting information about the stolen cars. Now, did you receive no responses from any of those people to that one dispatch alone?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I see the document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sure. It's 1D93, I believe, was the one I showed you, dated the 29th of July. It's tab 44 in your binder. And, by my count, it goes out to 12 different SJBs. Did none of them respond to you between 29 July and the end of October 1992?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me assist you to understand this part as well. The Security Services Centre of Romanija-Bircani area, dealt with the TAS factory matters. The information arrived via a collated document sent by that centre. The organisational system was such that the information was sent to the centre. Through various reports coming from stations, through dispatches, via courier and through other means, all of this arrived to the Sarajevo-Birac CSB, and all of this information was then sent in one report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So you're saying that if there were any responses from those 12, 11 or 12, SJBs they all sat in CSB Sarajevo until sometime when they were collated and put together and sent to you as one document. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Because when we were supposed to draft a review, since the Sarajevo, Romanija, and Birac centre did not have all of the information compiled in one place, I sent the dispatch to all of their stations and to the police detachment which was attached to that centre. Its headquarters were within the centre. I think that the centre then sent out more extensive report, stating that the Sekovici station knew nothing concerning that. Or some other station.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me go to something else. You were asked about the situation where certain individuals who had been relieved of their duties in -- in the ministry and put at the disposal of the army, what happened to those persons, if there were any pending criminal proceedings in place at that time? You were asked whether those criminal proceedings terminated because they'd been relieved of their documents, and you said no. My question is: What happened to any ongoing criminal proceedings against a person, for example, a reserve MUP policeman, who had been relieved of his duties and put at the disposal of the army and sent off to the front line. What happened to pending criminal proceedings against a person like that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is the prosecutor's office that is in charge of criminal proceedings. If an instigation was commenced pursuant to the prosecutor's request, then it is an investigative judge who has to undertake certain steps. And then once the indictment is confirmed, court proceedings are instituted. The minister of the interior could not affect, nor did it have any authority to affect the work of judicial organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm trying to understand though how -- how it played out in real life, because I see what, in English, I would call a Catch-22 situation. Reserve policemen engages in some kind of conduct, criminal conduct, that results in proceedings being initiated against him, which would have been in a civilian court, right, if it was for something he did while he was a reserve policeman. The criminal proceedings would be in a civilian court, rather than a military court. Right so far?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If the crime was committed in the territory of the municipality which is not in the war zone, because any area that is part of a war zone falls under the military jurisdiction. In the war zone, every policemen is resubordinated to the military command, and it is the military rules that are in effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, we may have some disagreement about that. And we'll talk about that later. But a reserve policeman who has been subjected to criminal proceedings in a civilian court who, in the meantime, because, as we all know, criminal proceedings often take a long time to go through the process, in the meantime he has been taken off by the army and he is on the front line. Now, when he is under the army and on the front line, the civilian court don't have any jurisdiction over him at that moment, do they? Because he is in the army fighting at the front line.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: If a person committed a crime as a civilian, then, naturally, the civilian prosecutor's office and the court would have jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But my point is: In the meantime, after the proceedings have started and before they are completed, that person has been taken off by the army and is fighting at the front line. Now, how does the civilian court get a hold of him because is he in the army? And wouldn't the army say, No, no, don't touch that guy. He's working for me right now. Isn't that how it worked in real life?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: If any soldier or military commander did something of that sort, I simply don't know about it, and I couldn't speculate about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. But I mean, civilian courts didn't have any jurisdiction over -- of the RS member; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm -- I'm -- I'm wondering what is the basis of Mr. Hannis's question. We know that the witness is not -- is not a lawyer. This is a strictly legal question, the question of jurisdiction. I don't know ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I don't know what Mr. Hannis's intention was, but the impression I had was about what happened in practice, not so much the -- the -- strict legal principles. Did I misunderstand you, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I'm trying to find out, as Judge Harhoff often does, is, we know what it says in the law but what happened in real life.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but, Your Honours, that is precisely -- understanding this, I didn't object before. But this question is: "I mean, civilian courts didn't have any jurisdiction over the RS member; right?" That was the question and that is why I objected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I understand, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. I take it, Mr. Macar, you wouldn't know the answer to that question; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you would be so kind to repeat the question. I wasn't focussed enough, and I'm experiencing some problems. So would you please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I will. I noticed that you were holding your back earlier. Do you want to have an earlier break?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we could go into closed session and I will explain what I have to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, we go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back to open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we would resume at, say, 4.50.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We will report to counsel as to how we've resolved these matters, but it probably should be in private session, so we'll wait until the witness comes back into court.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Macar, I'd like to show you now Exhibit 1D176. I think this is in tab 41 of your binder. It was a Defence document. You see this is the -- an order from Mr. Stanisic dated the 27th of July, 1992. And the preamble says, in my English: "In accordance with the order by the President of the Presidency ... and the request of the Assembly of the Serbian people which was in session on 25 and 26 July 1992, I hereby order ..." And number 4 in the order is: "Immediately disband and place under the command of the army of the Serbian republic all special units formed during the war in the areas of Security Services Centres." One of my first question is: Do you know what is referred to as the order by the President of the Presidency? Did you ever see what that order was and what it said specifically?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the order issued by the President of the Presidency. And I don't know its context, and I don't know the format in which it was written.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't know that we have seen it in this trial so far either. You said at page 22960, when asked about this item 4, you said the reason for disbanding of the special units was done "because the ministry never approved their establishment. Their members had not been vetted, and they didn't have decisions on appointment from the ministry headquarters." Now, this order makes reference to, in addition to the President's order that we don't know what it says, makes reference to the request of the Assembly, which was in session on 25 and the 26 July. I understand from your prior answers that you did not attend that session of the Assembly on 25 and 26 July; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you just tell me where it was held and then I will be able to give you an answer? Because that's how I remember them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: My notes indicate that was held in the Jahorina, Hotel Bistrica. And I think you said you weren't sure about that one, is actually what you said.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I was not sure. I said I might have been present.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Now given the fact that we have this order, which includes an order to immediately disband the special units, does that refresh your memory about what -- whether you might have attended the session, in that there might been some discussion about criminal behaviour of special police units or anything of that nature? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the topic related to the crime enforcement section, then I would like to see the items on the agenda that pertained to the work of the ministry; and if there was anything that had to do with the crime police, then I could tell you, with greater certainty, whether I was present there or not. And the order to disband special units was not issued because there were some reports about crimes committed by those units or individuals from those units. That was not the only reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I'm willing to agree with you that that may not have been the only reason, if you'll agree with me that it was one of the reasons. Can you do that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The primary reason - this is what I knew - was that the special units had to transform and had to be put under the control of the MUP headquarters. In the course of April and May, the centres set up those special units and the senior officers and rank-and-file personnel of those units were not verified by the ministry headquarters. And the concept, according to which those units were used, because when this order was issued, the concept was put together whereby special units were to be used primarily for security and also as a -- combat units, to take part in the fighting, under the command of the Republika Srpska army and in line with the Law on National Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But the -- it seems unlikely that the Presidency order -- or, the requests from the Assembly would have been based upon knowing that the proper procedure had not been followed in the MUP but, rather, the fact that some of those special units and some individuals in some of those special units were engaging in crimes. Would you agree with me about that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in the course of your inspection tours carried out by -- by the inspectors in the CSBs and the SJBs later in the year, did you not hear about; for example, crimes, including murders committed by the special unit from Banja Luka, during operations in Kotor Varos earlier in the year? You didn't hear reports about that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Let's look at tab 58 in your binder. This is Exhibit P605. And this is actually from Mr. Zupljanin in the Banja Luka CSB forwarding to his SJBs an order of the minister which talks about, item number 2: "The Serbian army is directly responsible for ... security of collection centres." And: "In the event that it should lack manpower ... war time assignments should be allotted." Did you see that; and were you aware of this order?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The order of the minister, as I have already noted -- well, I saw it not in August, but when the decision was made, and that was in September; the decision to relocate the MUP headquarters to Bijeljina. In order to prepare for the establishment of the crime police in the headquarters, and this went parallel with reporting to the minister, the purpose was to take, as soon as possible, measures to visit the CSBs and SJBs. And to this end, I put together the list of the CSBs and all the SJBs that belonged to them. I collected some data from the analysis section and the office of the ministry. The data pertained to the orders and demands that were sent to the centres and the reports that we received from the centres regarding the security situation in the field. And that's when I became acquainted with the minister's order.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. You mean this order that we've just been looking at; right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The order of the minister that Mr. Zupljanin conveyed to the offices out in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in the order immediately after item number 2, it talks about "disciplinary and, if need be, other measures should be taken against those who fail to obey the above order." Related to that, Mr. Zecevic had asked you to explain why this order and some of the others that you had been looked at prior were going out -- why there were so many of these orders going out, emphasising the responsibility of employees and these constant threats made of disciplinary and other measures. And your answer, page 22964, line 12 was: "Generally speaking, the interior minister, Mr. Stanisic, was very consistent in his application of the law." And I guess I would agree with you, to the extent that he was very consistent in issuing warnings about the failure to obey orders, because we have seen a number of documents where he does that. But, Mr. Macar, I would suggest to you that he was not consistent in following up on those warnings and disciplining people who violated them, such as Mr. Drljaca, Mr. Koroman, and others. Do you agree with me about that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't say that the minister wasn't consistent in following, following up, because the minister or any other single person cannot check on everything on their own. There are all those CSBs that need to carry out certain checks, pursuant to the powers they have. We talked about the problems. Now, I'm speaking in hypothetical terms. If there was an order issued that something needed to be done within eight days, that doesn't mean that, be it either due to the war activities or any other problems, that that was a realistic deadline. Sometimes there were objective reasons why a -- disciplinary proceedings could not be undertaken against somebody who did not abide by the eight-day deadline because there could have been some very valid reasons why they did not comply with the deadline. And this is quite a complex process that cannot be completed within 24 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me try and pose the question this way and -- and bear with me. I know you are a parent. You have children. I have children. We both have been children of parents, and let me give you the example of a parent who constantly is warning a child not to do something and threatening that, If you do that, I'm going to spank you, or I'm going to ground you, or I'm going take away your allowance. But if there are repeated threats made over time and there is never any action taken out, isn't it often the common result that the person warned the child or the employee or the policeman, if there are constant threats, but when the rules are broken and no discipline is enforced then an attitude is created where the child or the employee, or the policeman thinks, Ah, well, he doesn't really mean it, nothing is going to happen, so I don't have to pay any attention to that. Are you familiar with that phenomenon?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did have some problems with failing to punish my daughter in my family life. But, as far as the ministry's concerned, I know that disciplinary proceedings were conducted and that some employees were punished. We did not keep records of that in the crime police, because I'm anticipating your question. But the influence of the ministry and the CSBs towards the public security stations, which was not in line with the Law on the Interior, on internal affairs, and if in a station, senior officers were selected and appointed by institutions that were not part of the ministry, well, you could not really institute disciplinary proceedings against them. And, as regards the question whether the minister took measures. Yes, he often, not only threatened. In fact, his management style was that at each and every meeting he would make very energetic demands, and he did not threaten people with disciplinary proceedings. He said, You would be dismissed, unless you do this or that. And I think that I tried to apply the same standard, the same treatment to my subordinates. But on the ground, where the ministry did not have an influence, I don't know who was in a position to institute disciplinary proceedings when those people were outside of the legal framework of the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you this then: You know who Stevo Todorovic was in Bosanski Samac; yes?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stevan Todorovic was the station chief in Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And we've had some evidence that he had not been initially appointed by the ministry, but, rather, had been appointed by the local Crisis Staff. Is that consistent with your information?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learnt that from a report filed by the crime police officers who had visited the Doboj CSB.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And we've had a suggestion or some evidence that because he had not been appointed by the ministry, the ministry could not remove him. Is that what you were just explaining before now? Is that your understanding of how it worked? Because he hadn't been appointed by the ministry, he couldn't be removed by the ministry.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that, in this context, I did not say -- or, if I did, let me correct myself. I remember from the reports of the joint group that went there and some crime police personnel, that, primarily, there was a political problem in Samac because of the Crisis Staff which made it impossible to remove Mr. Todorovic from office. And I know that the Doboj CSB chief, Andrija Bjelosevic, had problems likewise in implementing the orders that had come from the minister, in terms of proposals for the appointment of personnel on the orders of the minister. Now, as for how it proceeded, I know only what was reported in the reports filed by the crime police because the crime police chief did not have the power to appoint or dismiss police station chiefs and commanders, so I really could not tell you what happened afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I'm still not sure I'm clear. Who did have the power to remove a police chief, a SJB chief, like Mr. Todorovic. Who had that power? Was it the CSB chief, or the minister, or both?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, we have seen an order by the minister, whereby he transfers some of the powers for the appointment of chiefs to the centre chiefs because of the situation, the fact that the territory was not contiguous, but the selection of the personnel was done by the minister. Because of the problems that we have already seen, the influence of the Crisis Staffs, some of the Crisis Staffs, on the appointment of personnel in some municipalities was so great that not only did they disrupt the normal procedure for the dismissal of people from office, but they were prepared to cause large-scale incidents in order to prevent the dismissal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, there's -- there is one intervention in the transcript. It says here, line 23, page 48: "The fact that the territory was not contiguous, but the selection of the personnel was done by the minister." That is not what the witness said. Maybe you can clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Macar, you heard what Mr. Zecevic said. Do you understand that and can you clarify?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have understood. I think that I said that the minister conveyed via his order part of the powers to the chiefs of CSBs when it comes to proposing personnel for the positions of the chief of stations and other senior positions. The order was a result -- the order was adopted as a result of the fragmentation of the territory and the inability to reach all SJBs from the headquarters and also the inability to timely exchange information, reports, and so on. This is what explains it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. But I'm -- I'm not clear. I know -- I think I know the order you're talking about. It was from late April, where Minister Stanisic issued this order delegating his authority regarding selections of certain employees to the CSB chiefs. Are we talking about the same thing?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question? I couldn't hear the interpreter quite well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Could we put up 1D73, which was at Defence tab 15. I think it's tab 15 in your binder, Mr. Macar. Is that the one that you were talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, having that in mind, and the circumstance in Bosanski Samac, for example, Mr. Todorovic was apparently appointed as SJB head in Samac by the local Crisis Staff. And, therefore, he wasn't appointed by the CSB chief, Mr. Bjelosevic, who was the person to whom the authority would have been applicable given this decision by Mr. Stanisic. Am I write so as far? I see you nod your head, but I need you to answer out loud.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In April, the ministry did not verify, confirm the position of the chief of the station in Brod. The Ministry of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, as it was known at the time. I also know that Mr. Andrija Bjelosevic had huge problems with the Crisis Staff in Bosanski Samac, when he attempted to implement the lawful procedures and announce the removal of Mr. Todorovic from office. Now, as for the details of that entire situation, I wouldn't be able to tell you, because I knew about the problems with Samac from the reports of inspectors who went to that SJB. But I know personally that Andrija Bjelosevic encountered huge problems in removing Todorovic from his position.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: As far as you know, there was no legal impediment. There was nothing in the Law on Internal Affairs that prevented Mr. Bjelosevic from removing Mr. Todorovic; right? It was a practical problem, a political problem, or a public-support-in-Samac problem, but not a legal impediment.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: As an economist, I will try to give you an answer. Any change entails certain preparations to pass a decision, stating that from this day on, it is not Goran Macar who is chief of the station, but, rather, Zoran Macar. Unless the Crisis Staff accepts it, the Crisis Staff who supports Mr. Todorovic -- or, rather, if Mr. Todorovic is also a member of the Crisis Staff, and if there is an event that disrupts the security situation in Samac, or if he manages to affect or influence certain persons in the military, then the paper alone has no force. Moreover, transformation of special units and creation of a new special unit under the command of the Ministry of the Interior was done precisely in order to attempt to improve the security situation on the ground and also to ensure that CSBs had all the support of the ministry when it comes to personnel changes whenever it was expected that some problems could erupt. For example, Andrija Bjelosevic went there on his own, and he faced threats, and so on. And the intention of the ministry could not be implemented without causing trouble. I'm now talking about practical problems encountered on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But the fact that it may have caused trouble is not a justification to do your duty, is it? I mean, a bank robber may have the support of his 16 cousins with shotguns, but that is not a reason that you shouldn't go out and arrest him if you know that he committed the bank robbery. It's part of the job; right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not a good example, the example of removal of the head of the police station. If somebody, due to objective reasons, is unable to undertake measures and activities that would cause graver problems, then perhaps - I'm now speaking as an ordinary man -- then perhaps that could be postponed by a day or two. This question is not properly addressed to me because I worked in the crime police. It would have been properly addressed to somebody else from the ministry. What I'm giving you now is simply my view of the things because within my powers, I could not remove head of the SJB. So I'm just giving you my personal view.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. But let's see if can you agree with me about this. Had the information that Mr. Todorovic was not appointed by the ministry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Have we not reached the end of how far we can get with Mr. Todorovic? And is it really relevant to push on with this matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, if you're satisfied it is clear about who had the authority to remove someone and the fact that removal wasn't done, then I can stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I think that has been cleared.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: If you're now moving on to something else, perhaps we should take the break, the final break for the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Macar, it's correct that under the Law on Internal Affairs for Republika Srpska - I believe it's Article 41 - that provides that the minister is the one who shall decide which employees will be considered authorised officials; right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the law by heart. Can you read it out to me?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. This is under Article 41, and the third paragraph in my English translation says: "The minister shall decide which employees will be considered authorised officials." Do you have any reason to disagree with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It is P181. I believe the witness asked to see the -- the law --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: My translation was: Could I read it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If you'd like to see it, I have it as Exhibit P530, 5-3-0. If we could [Overlapping speakers] witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we have P530. And in English, I'm at page 6. And I'm not sure where Article 41 is in the B/C/S. It may be the same. And if we could zoom in.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you see that, Mr. Macar? I think it's the third paragraph.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Would you agree, did I read it correctly?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]... Thank you. Now, let me show -- let me show you a document that you were showed on July the 7th. Page 22967. Exhibit 1D522, which is tab 88 in your binder, Mr. Macar. And this was a document that you talked about going from Minister Stanisic to the municipal assemblies, and the president, and the chairman of the Executive Committee. It's not clear to me, was this addressed to all municipal assemblies? Only to Bijeljina? Can you tell from looking at the document?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says here: "To the municipal assembly, to everyone, the president, and chairman of the Executive Committee."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But can you help me? Was it to all municipal assemblies in the Republika Srpska? Was that intended?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say. I didn't work either in the communications department, nor was I involved in any way in sending out documents, and I can't see on the face of it how it was sent. Given that it's November, and this is not an original dispatch, I would like to know who signed it. I think that this number indicates that this may have come from the analysis department.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, I see it has the number 10-013-441 at the top. And you've told us before that 10 pertains to the analysis administration. Is this a teletype, this format? This looks like a teletype to me.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say whether it was sent via regular mail, via a courier, or whether this is a dispatch. I can't see.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you see at the bottom the name Stanisic. It has two Ss and two Is. And one of the communications witnesses, I think, told us that that's an indication it was by teletype. That's how the diacritic in the Serbian language was represented. So Stanisic would have two Ss and two Cs. Does that help?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Because there were also typewriters where we had problems with the diacritics.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you -- did you personally regularly handle teletypes to know what they looked like, in terms of the format?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, as for those details, if -- if my name was written with a C instead of a Ch, I would automatically read it as it should be spelled. So I never paid attention to those minor details. I know that we have electrical typewriters that were faulty when it comes to diacritics.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If you take a look at the last paragraph, my English translation says: "Proceeding from this, as representatives of organs of civil [sic] authorities in the personnel recommendation procedure in the SJB in your municipality, you need to submit your recommendations, suggestions and opinions to the chief of CSB ... responsible for your area and to reach agreement on recommended candidates." First of all, that reads to me like this document was intended for all the municipal assemblies, not just one. It seems to be phrased in the collective rather than individual sense. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
